meta.description: Verified: Bill Gates wrote it. The line is a 'Business Lessons' bullet closing Chapter 11 of Business @ the Speed of Thought (Warner Books, 1999).
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Your most unhappy customers are your greatest source of learning'?
meta.ogDescription: It checks out. Bill Gates wrote it in Business @ the Speed of Thought (1999), as a bullet in the summary closing Chapter 11, 'Convert Bad News to Good'.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Confirmed in the book. It is the second of three “Business Lessons” bullets closing Chapter 11, “Convert Bad News to Good,” of Business @ the Speed of Thought (Warner Books, 1999), written with Collins Hemingway. Searching inside the book ↗ returns the sentence verbatim, directly after “Embrace bad news to learn where you need the most improvement.”

source.heading: The passage in the book

docMeta.dd: Business @ the Speed of Thought: Using a Digital Nervous System
11 — “Convert Bad News to Good,” in the closing “Business Lessons” summary

source.excerpt:
You should examine customer complaints more often than company financials. And your digital systems should help you convert bad news to improved products and services.

Business Lessons
• Embrace bad news to learn where you need the most improvement.
• Your most unhappy customers are your greatest source of learning.
• Implement policy and business structures that tie complaints directly to a fast solution.
trail: Wikiquote ↗ carries the line in its sourced 1990s section for Gates, credited to Business @ The Speed of Thought (1999) — but its only citation is a link to Microsoft’s long-dead marketing site for the book, with no chapter and no page. That is a starting point, not proof.

Searching inside the book settles it. Google Books ↗ returns one hit for the exact sentence, between “Embrace bad news to learn where you need the most improvement” and “Implement policy and business structures that tie complaints directly to a fast solution” — a three-bullet “Business Lessons” box, immediately followed by the section “Diagnosing Your Digital Nervous System.”

Microsoft’s own companion website for the book, captured in 2002 ↗, fixes the setting: Chapter 11 is “Convert Bad News to Good,” and its published excerpt closes on the sentence that runs straight into the bullets — “You should examine customer complaints more often than company financials.”

The edition is pinned by the catalogue record at the Internet Archive ↗: Business @ the speed of thought: using a digital nervous system, Bill Gates and Collins Hemingway, Warner Books, New York, 1999, ISBN 0446525685.

author.name: Bill Gates
author.heading: Who wrote it
author.metaLine: b. 1955 · Microsoft co-founder · author of The Road Ahead and Business @ the Speed of Thought
author.bio: Bill Gates co-founded Microsoft in 1975 and was its chief executive until 2000, afterwards serving as chief software architect and chairman. Business @ the Speed of Thought, written with Collins Hemingway and published in 1999, followed The Road Ahead (1995); its argument is that a company should build a “digital nervous system” so information moves as fast as the decisions that depend on it. Since stepping back from Microsoft he has worked chiefly through the Gates Foundation.

context.heading: Why the line is sharper than it looks
lead: The sentence is not a stray motivational aphorism — it is the compressed conclusion of an argument. Chapter 11 of Business @ the Speed of Thought is called “Convert Bad News to Good,” and per Microsoft’s own summary of it ↗ the chapter walks through a history of Microsoft’s failures, Promus Hotels turning service-guarantee complaints into action, and Microsoft Technical Support routing customer grievances back into product changes. Inside the chapter one section is headed, flatly, “Bad news must travel fast.”

Read in that setting, the famous line is an instruction about plumbing rather than attitude. Gates’s point is that complaints are the highest-signal data a company receives and that most firms never get them to the people who could act — which is why the bullet immediately after it is about structures that “tie complaints directly to a fast solution,” and why the same chapter says you should examine customer complaints more often than company financials.
detailsBody: Microsoft ran a companion website for the book at microsoft.com/billgates/speedofthought, with a summary and excerpts for each of the 23 chapters. It went offline years ago, and Wikiquote still cites that dead URL as the source for this quotation — which is why the line so often circulates with a book title attached but no chapter and no page. The site survives in the Wayback Machine, including a supplementary essay for Chapter 11 ↗ on using digital feedback from unhappy customers to improve products before a complaint is ever filed.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote's sourced 1990s section for Bill Gates contains the line "Your most unhappy customers are your greatest source of learning", cited to Business @ The Speed of Thought (1999) via a link to Microsoft's book website, with no chapter or page.

A search inside this edition of Business @ the Speed of Thought returns one verbatim hit for "Your most unhappy customers are your greatest source of learning", adjacent to "Embrace bad news to learn where you need the most improvement", "Implement policy and business structures that tie complaints directly to a fast solution", a "Business Lessons" heading and the following section "Diagnosing Your Digital Nervous System".

Microsoft's archived companion site identifies Chapter 11 as "Convert Bad News to Good", summarises it (Microsoft failures, Promus Hotels, Microsoft Technical Support converting complaints into product improvements), and ends its excerpt with "You should examine customer complaints more often than company financials. And your digital systems should help you convert bad news to improved products and services."

Microsoft's archived "Preempt Bad News Through Smart Software" page states that Chapter 11 of Business @ the Speed of Thought, "Convert Bad News to Good News", is about using digital feedback from unhappy customers to improve products or services.

The Internet Archive record lists Business @ the speed of thought: using a digital nervous system by Bill Gates (1955-) and Collins Hemingway, published by Warner Books, New York, 1999, ISBN 0446525685.
Wikipedia gives Bill Gates's birth date as October 28, 1955, his Microsoft CEO tenure as 1975-2000, and lists Business @ the Speed of Thought among his writings.
Wikipedia's article on Business @ the Speed of Thought identifies the authors as Bill Gates and Collins Hemingway and the publication year as 1999.
Microsoft's book-site chapter list and the Google Books table of contents both place "Convert Bad News to Good" as Chapter 11, immediately before "Know Your Numbers" (Chapter 12).
